Renewed global inflationary pressures, geopolitical tensions, and decreased fiscal space continued to put substantial pressure on the external debt positions of low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) in 2025. LMICs’ external borrowing levels reached a record $9.4 trillion at the end of the year, increasing 5.5 percent from $8.9 trillion in 2024. LMIC external debt has grown about 60 percent over the past decade, and the 2025 increase was the largest since the easing of the COVID-19 pandemic in 2021. The change in debt stock was driven by net debt inflows of $423.5 billion, a more than twofold increase from 2024, as well as by some debt forgiveness and the upward accounting effect of US dollar depreciation. During the first half of 2025, the US dollar experienced its biggest depreciation against other currencies in more than five decades, and the increase in new debt flows went largely to middle-income countries (MICs), predominantly because of continued support from multilateral creditors and a rebound in lending from private creditors. That rebound, driven by both new borrowing and buyback operations, indicated a recovery of investor confidence after a retrenchment by private lenders from 2022 to 2023 and only a small increase in 2024, as well as a renewed search for yield (table 1.1). This pattern shows the procyclical nature of the private creditor lending. It expands in favorable global conditions and contracts sharply when conditions tighten. (Refer to box 1.1 for definitions of debt terms used in this report.)

question: Under the G-7 Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) initiative, how are the loans to Ukraine serviced, and why are they still recorded as Ukraine's external debt?
answer:
Under the G-7 Extraordinary Revenue Acceleration (ERA) initiative, the loans to Ukraine are serviced from future revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets, not from Ukraine’s own budget. Those revenues are channeled through the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism, administered by the European Commission, and are used to pay principal and interest [idr:p039:text:1] (page 39, Chapter 1).

They are still recorded as Ukraine’s external debt because ERA support is extended as loans that create a repayment obligation for the government of Ukraine. Under the Debtor Reporting System and international statistical standards, the loan is classified as a debt instrument because there is a contractual obligation to repay principal and/or interest, regardless of the expected source of repayment. The report says that proceeds from immobilized or seized assets provide the mechanism for repayment but do not change the nature of the liability; only if repayment were legally limited to those proceeds, with no obligation for Ukraine to cover any shortfall, would the statistical treatment differ [idr:p039:text:1] (page 39, Chapter 1).

What is unique about this mechanism, compared to direct lending, is that the principal and interest are serviced from future revenues generated by immobilized Russian sovereign assets rather than from Ukraine’s own budget. ERA support extended as loans creates a repayment obligation for the government of Ukraine and is therefore recorded as an external debt liability, whereas the Ukraine Loan Cooperation Mechanism represents a financial asset of Ukraine available to service the loan. Under the Debtor Reporting System and international statistical standards—the Balance of Payments and International Investment Position Manual, sixth and seventh editions (IMF 2009, 2025) and External Debt Statistics: Guide for Compilers and Users (IMF 2014)— this loan is classified as a debt instrument based on the existence of a contractual obligation to repay principal and/or interest, rather than on the expected source of repayment. Accordingly, borrowing remains a debt liability even when debt service is expected to be financed from proceeds of immobilized or seized assets. Those proceeds provide the mechanism for repayment but do not change the nature of the liability.
